query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra‐thin, nanometer‐scale Ni-based coating on tungsten surfaces in conventional W–Cu composites will form a graded interfacial region that both reduces electron scattering and lowers the thermal boundary resistance, thereby enhancing thermal conductivity while maintaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance under fusion‐reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite in which tungsten and copper phases contact directly, exhibiting high interfacial electron scattering and appreciable thermal boundary resistance that compromise heat transfer.
generation.intervention: Prior to copper infiltration, deposit an ultra-thin (on the order of nanometers) high-electron-mobility Ni-based interlayer onto the tungsten surfaces.
generation.conditions: The composite is intended for fusion‐reactor joint applications, where it is subjected to high thermal flux, temperature cycling, and high-energy neutron/ion irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni-based interlayer facilitates the creation of a graded interface between tungsten and copper. This graded interface improves electron transport while preserving the mechanical bonding, essentially acting as a bridge that mitigates the interface mismatches.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale Ni coating enhances the electronic compatibility between tungsten and copper by reducing the interfacial mismatch and electron scattering. The improved electron transport across the interface lowers the thermal boundary resistance, leading to an overall increase in thermal conductivity. Simultaneously, the interlayer maintains or even strengthens the bonding between phases, preserving mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated W–Cu composite is expected to exhibit a significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to an unmodified composite, without detriment to its mechanical strength or resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
generation.baseline: A comparable W–Cu composite processed without the Ni-based interlayer treatment.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated under conditions mimicking fusion‐reactor environments. However, the optimal thickness of the Ni-based coating and its long-term stability under repetitive thermal and irradiation cycling remain to be precisely determined.
generation.uncertainty: The absolute magnitude of the thermal conductivity boost and the long-term performance of the ultra-thin interlayer under extended irradiation cycles are uncertain and require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set with the ultra-thin Ni-based coating on tungsten and a control set with the standard, unmodified tungsten surface. Process both sets identically in terms of copper infiltration and overall composite fabrication. Subject the samples to a suite of tests simulating fusion-reactor conditions, including high thermal flux, temperature cycling, and irradiation with neutrons or surrogate ions.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (using techniques such as laser flash analysis)
Mechanical durability (via tensile, compression, or fatigue testing)
Irradiation resistance (analyzing changes in microstructure, hardness, and defect accumulation post-irradiation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated W–Cu composite does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity relative to the control without causing any measurable degradation in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, a novel HEA/diamond composite was studied by magnetron sputtering Ti/Ni coating and the spark plasma sintering (SPS) method. A Ti/Ni coating (inner Ti and outer Ni) of diamond particles was realized by magnetron sputtering. An HEA/coated diamond interface was obtained, composed of the solid solution formed by diffusion between the HEA matrix and Ni element in the outer layer of diamond particles. The carbide formed by the reaction of Ti element with diamond particles. On the one hand, this interface can effectively reduce the interface energy between diamond and the HEA matrix and improve the bonding strength. On the other hand, the cracks and micro-holes on the interface after SPS can be filled by generated carbides to improve the density of the composites and improve the strength, toughness and other mechanical properties of the composites.

Diamond single crystal particles with Ti/Ni coatings were obtained by magnetron sputtering. The diamond gained more than 30% weight and the coating thickness was 10–20 μm. The interfacial diffusion and solid solution formation in coated diamond composites led to the increase of interfacial bonding strength. The interface bonding strength and mechanical properties of the composites without diamond coating decreased, due to the occurrence of graphitization at the interface and the formation of carbides. Compared with the composite with uncoated diamond, the density, hardness, transverse fracture strength and interfacial bonding properties of the composite with coated diamond were significantly improved. The wear resistance of the coated composites is obviously higher than that of the uncoated composites, because the coating on the diamond particles maintains a relatively complete crystal form in the SPS process and has a higher bonding strength with the HEA matrix. This improves the holding force of the matrix and gives full play to the excellent properties of the HEA.

frame.system: Tungsten–copper metal‐matrix composite in its conventional state (with typical W and Cu phases forming a percolated or infiltrated microstructure) as used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint components.
frame.goal: To boost the composite’s thermal conductivity while simultaneously retaining its mechanical durability and resistance to irradiation.
frame.limitation: In current W–Cu composites, attempts to improve thermal conductivity often compromise mechanical integrity or irradiation tolerance, leaving no single intervention that addresses all three functional requirements simultaneously.
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
The intervention must not diminish the material’s mechanical robustness or its performance under irradiation
The improvement must be applicable under the demanding conditions of heat‐dissipation and fusion‐reactor environments
regime: High thermal load conditions as found in heat-dissipation systems
Irradiation and fusion-reactor operational environments (which impose high-energy neutron or ion irradiation, temperature cycling, etc.)
prior_attempts: Optimizing the W-to-Cu ratio to balance conductivity and strength, which typically led to trade-offs between the properties
Introducing secondary phases or alloying elements; these approaches sometimes improved one property but at the cost of reducing either mechanical integrity or irradiation resistance
Microstructural control methods (e.g., directional solidification) that enhance connectivity for heat transfer but can induce anisotropy affecting mechanical properties

decision.trend: Early efforts in W–Cu composites focused on adjusting the phase ratios and introducing alloying elements or secondary phases to balance thermal conductivity with mechanical strength and irradiation resistance. Over time, researchers experimented with microstructural control methods—such as directional solidification—to improve heat‐transfer pathways, yet these often introduced anisotropy or interface weaknesses. More recently, studies on other composite systems (e.g., Ti/Ni‐coated diamond particles in high-entropy alloy matrices in PMC7514646 and refractory alloy designs in PMC11901246) have demonstrated that engineering the interface can enhance bonding and electron transport while preserving mechanical and irradiation properties.
decision.unsolved: No single intervention in W–Cu composites has yet overcome the inherent interfacial electron scattering and bonding challenges that limit thermal conductivity improvements while maintaining mechanical durability and radiation resistance under fusion‐reactor conditions.
decision.lever: Apply an ultra-thin, high-electron-mobility interlayer (e.g., a nanometer-scale Ni-based coating) onto tungsten surfaces prior to copper infiltration
decision.why: This approach follows the trend where interfacial treatments in composite systems improved both bonding and transport properties without sacrificing structural integrity. Such a coating is expected to reduce thermal boundary resistance between the tungsten and copper phases, facilitate electron transport for higher thermal conductivity, and preserve the mechanical and irradiation-resistance characteristics of the composite. Prior evidence from interface-engineered systems (as seen in PMC7514646) supports that a carefully chosen, nanoscale coating can act as a bridge between dissimilar phases, making it the most plausible next step for addressing the threefold property challenge in W–Cu composites.
